problem: End-to-end RL/IL ObjectNav policies memorize spatial patterns and fail to generalize to unseen scenes and novel object categories, while frozen VLM-based methods hallucinate and lack structured intermediate reasoning or any mechanism to handle incorrect reasoning.
motivation: Humans find objects by reasoning about object-object and object-scene co-occurrence rather than exhaustive exploration or SLAM. Injecting structured, multi-step commonsense reasoning into a small fine-tuned VLM, with noise-aware training, should improve zero-shot generalization to novel objects and layouts.
key_idea: Fine-tune a compact VLM on multi-turn hierarchical chain-of-thought QA data (perception then planning) derived from human demonstrations, with a confidence-weighted (sigmoid) loss that down-weights noisy or hallucinated reasoning samples.
insight: The ablation on MP3D Val (unseen scenes) shows that structure matters most: pure text 24.3% SR, standard CoT 36.5%, H-CoT 52.9%, and adding closed-loop confidence weighting gives 55.2%. So most of the gain comes from hierarchical decomposition into room-level and object-level reasoning, and confidence weighting adds a smaller but consistent gain. Data scaling saturates (35k to 70k), which suggests reasoning supervision matters more than more demonstrations.
method: H-CoT Perception Rounds: multi-turn QA on the egocentric RGB image that identifies subgoal objects and layout, guesses the room type from object co-occurrence, and relates detected objects to the target via commonsense, with per-object relevance scores.

H-CoT Planning Rounds: reasons over the accumulated context to judge whether the current room is plausible for the target, suggests high-level moves (e.g. 'explore another room', 'turn around') that are discretized into text actions aligned with the human demonstration action.

Annotation pipeline: human demonstrations from MP3D-HD-70k are annotated offline by pretrained models (Qwen-VL-Chat for subgoal detection, Qwen-7B for semantic guesswork/association, ChatGPT-3.5-turbo for action suggestion and scene reasoning) into multi-turn QA data.
Confidence scoring: each QA trajectory gets a score c_i in [0,1] from the agreement between the parsed final suggested action and the human GT action, combined with detection certainty.
Adaptive loss: cross-entropy weighted by sigmoid(alpha*(c_i - beta)) so that high-confidence samples dominate and hallucinated ones are suppressed.
Policy fine-tuning: InternVL2 2B VLM fine-tuned with LoRA (r=8, alpha=16, lr 3e-4, batch 16, 3 epochs, 4 V100s, ~19h on 50k) to output actions; inference for multi-turn takes ~1.2 s.

setting.backbone: InternVL2-2B (LoRA fine-tuned); QA annotation done with Qwen-VL-Chat, Qwen-7B, ChatGPT-3.5-turbo
setting.training_data: MP3D-HD human demonstrations (35k/50k/70k cleaned subsets, 28/40/56 scenes) converted to multi-turn QA with confidence scores; object-generalization uses 16 seen classes (MP3D-HD-35k-C16, 20,595 episodes)
setting.observation: egocentric RGB (plus depth and odometry available on the agent); target category given
setting.action_space: 6 discrete actions: move_forward 25 cm, turn_left/right 30°, look_up/down 30°, stop
setting.privileged: none at test time (human demonstrations and LLM-generated annotations used only in training)

numbers.extra: trained on 35k human demos (28 scenes); evaluated on unseen scenes of MP3D-Val (11 scenes, 2,195 episodes); 500-step limit

numbers_note: The paper's abstract claims a 22.4% improvement in SR and SPL, but the tables are inconsistent about scale: the training table SPL is printed as fractions (0.38) while the zero-shot table uses percent. The 'Training Results' table appears to evaluate on training data, so it is not a true val-unseen result. Zero-shot results use a custom split and are not the standard Habitat ObjectNav challenge.
results: CL-CoTNav (35k demos) reaches 55.2% SR / 25.7% SPL on novel objects and 58.5% / 27.4% on novel scenes, versus the strongest baseline DivScene at 44.1/19.1 and 46.7/21.3. Ablation shows H-CoT gives the largest gain (52.9% SR) and closed-loop weighting adds a further 2.3 points.
limitations: Relies on imitation learning, so it is bounded by the quality and coverage of the demonstrations; the annotation depends on noisy LLM-generated labels
Evaluated only in simulation (Habitat MP3D), with no real-robot validation
Multi-turn inference costs ~1.2 s per step and metric scales/eval protocols are inconsistent, complicating comparison with standard ObjectNav benchmarks
